props.title: Less Than Zero
props.initialSlug: Rich LA teens spiral into drugs and destruction

sections.content: Less Than Zero captures the hollow decadence of 1980s Los Angeles youth culture through a neon-lit nightmare of cocaine, failed dreams, and lost innocence. Robert Downey Jr. delivers a haunting breakthrough performance as Julian, a drug-addicted rich kid spiraling into debt and destruction. The film, while softening the brutality of Bret Easton Ellis's source novel, stands alongside Bright Lights, Big City (1988) and River's Edge (1986) as a defining chronicle of '80s youth alienation. Andrew McCarthy plays Clay, returning from college to find his best friend Julian and ex-girlfriend Blair (Jami Gertz) caught in a web of addiction and emptiness.

sections.content: Director Marek Kanievska bathes the film in stylish emptiness - modernist mansions, trendy nightclubs, and palm tree-lined streets that feel more menacing than glamorous. The soundtrack, featuring The Bangles' haunting cover of "Hazy Shade of Winter," perfectly captures the era's glossy despair. While Wall Street (1987) tackled '80s excess through high finance, Less Than Zero shows its impact on privileged youth left morally adrift by absent parents and too much money.

The film belongs to a vital subset of '80s cinema examining youth in crisis, alongside Rumble Fish (1983) and At Close Range (1986). These films shared a neo-noir aesthetic applied to teen narratives, creating a unique hybrid that influenced later works like The Rules of Attraction (2002), another Bret Easton Ellis adaptation. Downey Jr.'s performance is particularly poignant given his own subsequent struggles with addiction, lending the film an eerie prescience. SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence

sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond its immediate era, setting a template for countless stories of privileged youth in crisis. Thirteen (2003) and Alpha Dog (2006) follow its examination of Los Angeles youth culture gone wrong, while shows like "Euphoria" carry its aesthetic DNA. The film's unflinching look at addiction among the wealthy young presaged everything from Requiem for a Dream (2000) to Beautiful Boy (2018).
